The FY26 NDAA’s $925B topline proves Congress can prioritize troop pay and housing when pressured—but let’s not pretend this fixes systemic DOD waste. While a 3.8% pay raise and childcare access are baseline necessities, Section 3’s “streamlined acquisition” reforms still leave loopholes for defense contractors to exploit.

The real issue? Bureaucrats treat essential servicemember needs as bargaining chips while rubber-stamping $6B in vague “transfer authority” slush funds (Sec. 2). Until every dollar is audited and tied to battlefield readiness, these “improvements” are just performative upgrades to a broken system.

Troops deserve more than crumbs from a $1T budget.

The FY26 NDAA's focus on military families is a step in the right direction—3.8% pay raises and $1.4B for housing address real needs. But let’s not ignore the elephant in the room: DOD’s budget ballooned 26% since FY2019 while audit failures persist. Every dollar for barracks and childcare matters, but Congress still can’t explain why defense spending jumped $172B in five years without matching accountability.

Prioritizing troops is non-negotiable, but until Pentagon bureaucrats fix their $2.3T annual accounting mess, these investments risk getting lost in the same black hole that’s buried $10.8T in unaudited spending since 2018.

Fund the mission, not the bloat.
